background.definition: Hematuria is defined as the presence of RBCs in the urine, either visible (gross hematuria) or detected by direct microscopy (microscopic hematuria with 3 or more RBCs per high-power field).

list.listitem: The American Urologic Association (AUA) notes prevalence of microscopic hematuria varies between 2.4 to 31.1 % depending on the age, risk factors, and gender of the population studied.
Studies of general population health screening have found a prevalence between 2% and 20%.

Of patients referred for evaluation of hematuria for specialty care, 2% to 13% have a urologic malignancy. One study showed that rates of developing urologic cancer were the same among people with asymptomatic hematuria and no hematuria. The risk for progression is highest among older males.
Causes of asymptomatic microscopic hematuria range from minor, incidental findings that do not require treatment to highly significant lesions that immediately threaten the patient's life.
Hematuria can be broadly classified as nephrologic or urologic in origin.
See table for risk factors for hematuria.
The pathophysiology of hematuria depends on the anatomic site within the urinary tract from which blood loss occurs.

Blood originating from the nephron is termed nephrologic hematuria. RBCs can enter the urinary space from the glomerulus or the renal tubule. Finding casts in the urine connotes significant disease at the glomerular level. However, in disease of the nephron, casts can be absent, and isolated RBCs may be the only finding. The presence of proteinuria helps support a glomerular source of blood loss.

Anything that disrupts the uroepithelium such as irritation, inflammation, or invasion can result in morphic RBCs in the urine. This is termed urologic hematuria. Such insults may include malignancy, renal stones, trauma, infection, and medications.

list.listitem: It is initially important to exclude a UTI and blood contamination from menstruation, exercise, and sexual or physical trauma (eg, bicycle, "march" hematuria, etc.). Some medications and foods (e.g., beets) can also discolor the urine without causing true hematuria. Identifying significant high risk factors and distinguishing between nephrologic and urologic causes helps to guide the initial diagnostic process (see and ).
Pain, clots, and the shape of the clots associated with gross hematuria is very important for guiding further evaluation (see ).
Careful history of risk factors for malignancy, including tobacco use and family history of urologic malignancy, should be obtained.
Increased urinary frequency and dysuria suggest lower urinary tract pathology, such as bladder infection or bladder cancer.

Hematuria increases the likelihood of infection in women under age 50 years, but actually decreases in women over age 50 for whom other causes are more common. Hematuria in a man greatly increases the likelihood of a UTI (LR 29).
Gross blood at the initiation of voiding suggests a urethral pathology, whereas continuous hematuria suggests a renal, ureteral, or bladder problem.
Patients with microhematuria should be categorized as low, intermediate, or high risk for genitourinary malignancy, and this should guide subsequent diagnostics (see .

Urinary dipsticks can be very useful in the detection of asymptomatic microscopic hematuria, with a sensitivity of 91% to 100%. However, the specificity of urinary dipsticks is limited, ranging from 65% to 99% for 2 to 5 RBCs per high-power field. The dipstick cannot determine the origin of the bleeding. A positive urine dipstick with trace blood or more should prompt urinalysis. Providers should not diagnose microhematuria with positive dipstick alone.

Quantifying the amount of RBCs per high-power field can be helpful with suspected infection or renal lithiasis. Additionally, if acanthocytes make up >5% of RBCs, this can be a good marker of glomerular hematuria.
Further evaluation is not recommended for young women with hemorrhagic cystitis that clears after treatment.
A review of studies of women with microscopic hematuria concluded that the positive predictive value is very low: 859 women would require full evaluation to identify one malignancy.

In low-risk patients with microhematuria, urinalysis should be repeated in 6 months. If hematuria is found on repeat UA, then they should be considered intermediate or high risk and these patients should undergo appropriate cystoscopy and upper urinary tract imaging.
Hematuria can be monitored after ANCA-associated glomerulonephritis as a predictor of kidney outcome.
Intermediate-risk patients with hematuria should undergo cystoscopy and renal ultrasound, while high risk patients should undergo cystoscopy and CT urogram, MR urogram, or retrograde pyelogram.

In a retrospective review of 847 patients who underwent CT, ultrasound, cystoscopy and cytology for evaluation of hematuria. Of the 432 with microscopic hematuria, 7 (1.6%) had bladder cancer and 1 had renal cell cancer. Of those with visible hematuria, 14.9% were diagnosed with bladder cancer and 1.6% had renal cell cancer. Malignancy was more likely in those who were older, smoked, and had a lower BMI.
A review of case series reported that ureteroscopy could successfully be used to treat causes of benign essential hematuria such as hemangiomas and venous ruptures.
See for an overview of imaging modalities.

A prospective study of 115 patients with asymptomatic microscopic hematuria found that while overall costs were similar for IV pyelography (IVP) and CT, the CT was more accurate and identified important nonurologic diagnoses such as aneurysm.
Among 834 patients with renal colic and microscopic hematuria who had CT as their initial imaging study, 85% were diagnosed with renal lithiasis.

Ultrasound is the recommended test of choice in children with isolated hematuria. CT with contrast is preferable to ultrasound in children with painful (nontraumatic) hematuria. CT with contrast is recommended for painful traumatic hematuria in children.
Renal ultrasonography is the imaging of choice in intermediate-risk patients with hematuria due to its lower cost and absence of radiation compared to CT urogram.

Multidetector CT urography is relatively sensitive (64%) and highly specific (98%) for detecting urinary neoplasms. The positive predictive values and negative predictive values are 76% and 96%, respectively. It may serve as the primary imaging modality to evaluate patients with hematuria.

MRI is considered a problem-solving approach for patients who require additional imaging after CT or ultrasound. MR urography currently serves as an alternative imaging technique for children and pregnant women and for patients with a contraindication to iodinated contrast media.
If a patient has a contraindication to CT and MRI, they could undergo evaluation with retrograde pyelography with non-contrast axial imaging or renal ultrasound.
In intermediate-risk patients with hematuria who prefer to avoid cystoscopy, urine cytology and validated tumor marker testing, including UroVysion and Cxbladder Triage, can be undertaken.

UroVysion fluorescence in situ hybridization assay has been shown in studies to be more sensitive than voided cytology for detecting bladder cancer of all grades and stages in patients with either gross or microscopic hematuria.
OncoUrine, a tumor marker assay, was found to have an 80% sensitivity and 91.9% specificity for diagnosing bladder cancer.
Cxbladder Triage was found to have 90% sensitivity, 56% specificity.
A diagnostic algorithm for patients with asymptomatic microscopic hematuria (3 or more RBC/HPF) is shown in .
A simple, validated risk score can identify patients with microscopic hematuria who are at low (0-0.4%), moderate (0.2-3.1%) or high (1.3-6.3%) risk of malignancy.

Patients with gross hematuria should be regarded as having urologic malignancy until proven otherwise. Pain in association with gross hematuria usually results from upper urinary tract hematuria with obstruction of the ureters by clots (kidney tumor, upper urinary tract urothelial carcinoma). A diagnostic algorithm for patients with gross hematuria is shown in .

For patients with urologic malignancy, appropriate referrals should be made to urology and/or oncology. Chemotherapy, radiation, and surgery such as radical cystectomy may be indicated with good outcomes.

feature.caption: Imaging Modalities for Evaluation of Hematuria.

tr.td: IVU
In many centers, IVU remains the initial evaluation for upper tract imaging in patients with microscopic evaluation.
It has limited sensitivity in detecting small renal masses.
It cannot distinguish solid masses from cystic ones.
It is better than US for detection of urothelial carcinoma in kidney and ureter.
Ultrasonography (US)
US does not involve exposure to IV radiographic contrast medium.
US is appropriate for use during pregnancy.
US is an effective modality for the detection and characterization of renal cysts.
Its accuracy decreases considerably in the detection of solid renal lesions.
When US is used as the primary screening modality, the yield from imaging may be increased by adding a plain film of the abdomen.
CT
CT has increasingly been used either complementary to or instead of IVU.
It is less expensive and more widely available than MRI.
In the evaluation of suspected urinary stones, the non-contrast-enhanced spiral CT scan is superior to either IVU or US.
It is the preferred modality for detection and characterization of solid renal masses.
Multidetector CT urography is relatively sensitive and highly specific for detecting urinary neoplasms. It may serve as the primary imaging modality to evaluate patients with hematuria.
MRI
MRI is considered a problem-solving approach for patients who require additional imaging after CT or US.
MRI urography currently serves as an alternative imaging technique for children and pregnant women and for patients with a contraindication to iodinated contrast media.

Risk factors for urothelial cancer include irritative lower urinary tract symptomss, history of chemotherapy with cyclophosphamide or ifosfamide, history of pelvic radiation, family history of urothelial cancer or Lynch syndrome, occupational exposure to benzene or aromatic amine chemicals, history of chronic indwelling foreign body in urinary tract.
